title: Kindness spreads
hookLine: in lab games, generosity was passed on to others (Fowler and Christakis, 2010)

lines: PAY IT FORWARD, OR DRIVE OFF?
cards: The drive-through window slides open, and the cashier says the car ahead already paid. Maybe a small, odd jolt. Then a choice, right there with the engine running: pay for the car behind, or drive off with a free coffee.
Some people pay it forward, and the next driver gets the same jolt, and the same choice. Stories like this get passed around because they feel like proof of something.
So, plainly: when kindness lands on someone, does it actually travel on to the next person? And what does a lab have to say?

teach.b: First, the game. The researchers James Fowler and Nicholas Christakis used an economics game played by strangers.

Each round, a small group got some money and chose how much to put into a shared pot that benefited everyone. Then the groups were shuffled, so nobody played with the same people twice. Second, what they saw.

teach.h: GENEROSITY MOVED ON TO NEW PEOPLE.
teach.b: When someone was generous to a player in one round, that player tended to give more in later rounds, to brand new people, and those people in turn gave a little more to others.
Generosity reached people who had never met the first giver. The authors called it a cascade. Third, the honest size of it.

teach.h: A MODEST NUDGE, NOT A MIRACLE.
teach.b: This was a game with small amounts of money, played by people who would never meet, and the nudge each time was modest. It doesn't prove that one coffee changes a city.
It suggests something smaller and sturdier: being treated generously makes a person somewhat more likely to be generous next. Fourth, an old story with the same shape.
In the Acts of the Apostles, Paul and the other travelers are shipwrecked on the island of Melita.
The King James text says: "And the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one."
Behind the word kindness, the Greek has philanthropia, often rendered love of humankind. A fire for strangers, cold and wet.
A few verses later, Paul heals the sick on the island, and the islanders send the travelers on with what they need. Kindness given, kindness going on.

how: Some people make a habit of "paying it forward": answering a kindness by doing something kind for someone new.

o: kindness repaid only to the person who gave it
generosity received, then passed on to someone new
a rumor of good news moving through a town

p: generosity passed on to new people
a fire kindled for shipwrecked strangers

s: in the game, players were shuffled so they didn't meet the same people twice
that's what made it interesting: the generosity moved on to strangers.
the study proved one kind act can change a whole city
the nudge was modest, in a game with small amounts of money.
in Acts, the islanders of Melita kindled a fire for the shipwrecked travelers
the King James text calls it "no little kindness."

games.q: at the drive-through, the cashier says the car ahead paid for your coffee. what do you do?
o: pay for the car behind you.
do something kind for someone later today.
games.why: any of these is fine. the lab finding is about what tends to happen next: people treated generously often pass it on, and not always to the giver or right away.

practice: Bring to mind one kindness that landed on you recently, a held door, a patient answer, a message at the right moment, and let it be vivid for a few breaths: who, where, what it felt like to receive.
Then ask quietly, who is next, and rest with whatever face comes to mind, no grand gesture needed.

wordCard.voice: Kindness spreads. In the lab, people who were treated generously tended to pass generosity on to strangers. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from the New Testament's Acts 28:2, where the King James text renders it "kindness": the islanders' love for strangers.

carryVoice: Your line: it spreads. Every chain of kindness starts with one small link. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Fowler and Christakis, "Cooperative behavior cascades in human social networks" (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences)

sources.q: And the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one
